extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying infringement law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and tests for infringement of patents on machines, processes, manufactures, and compositions of matter, as derived from case law and treatise commentary. Focuses on when making, using, or selling constitutes infringement and related doctrines (intent, constructive use, product vs. machine, licenses, remedies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-use / making-for-test exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a patented machine for the mere purpose of experimenting on the sufficiency of the specification may not be injurious to the patentee; when no profits are taken, the making for experiment is distinguished from making for use or sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise notes conflicting authorities: Mr. Justice Washington held that testing the practical utility was no answer to a charge of 'using', while Mr. Justice Story held that making a patented machine is an infringement only when made for use or for sale. Use this as a fact-sensitive inquiry: pure, non-commercial experimental construction to test a specification may avoid liability; making with commercial intent likely does not. (See Whittemore v. Cutter and related authorities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent-to-infringe test for making
rubrics_metrics.description: "The test is, whether the party made the machine with an intent to infringe the patent right, and deprive the owner of the lawful rewards of his discovery."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the maker's motive and surrounding circumstances. Evidence of intent to deprive the patentee of lawful rewards (e.g., making for sale or use in competition) supports infringement; innocent, experimental, or non-commercial making may not. (Case law references discussed in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive using via purchase/contract
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who makes a machine in violation of the patentee's right, or purchases it from one who made it, and then hires it out or otherwise arranges for its use, may be held responsible for a 'using' of the machine (constructive use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The watch-chain case: where a purchaser contracted to buy manufactured chains from a maker who used the patented machine, the Supreme Court held a genuine contract and no other connection meant no 'use' by the purchaser; but a colorable contract, evidence of ownership, or a hire-for-term under color of sale with intent to invade the patent would amount to breach. Examine whether the transaction is real vs. a sham to conceal hiring/ownership. (See Keplinger v. De Young and related discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Using proved by personal use, employment of others, or profit
rubrics_metrics.description: "A using of a machine is to be taken as proved, either when the party charged has used it himself or has employed others to use it for him, or has profited by the use of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability may be found where defendant personally used the patented machine, directed employees/agents to use it, or obtained profits from its use. Even indirect participation or profiting can establish 'use'. (See Woodworth v. Hall and cited passages.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale must be of complete machine (not mere materials) to constitute infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be an infringement by 'sale', it must be something more than a sale of the materials, either separate or combined; it must be a sale of a complete machine, for use as a machine, which is patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sale of raw materials or parts—even complete materials sold by a sheriff on execution—has been held not to be an infringement if the seller did not purport to transfer the right to use the patented machine. Look for an express or implied right to use conveyed with the sale; absent that, vendor liability is unlikely. (Illustrated by sheriff's-sale authority in Sawin v. Guild and commentary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of a patented machine/process usually not an infringement of the machine/process patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of the articles produced by a patented machine, or by a process which is patented, is not an infringement of the patent on the machine (or process), except where the product itself is a new manufacture or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the claimed subject is a process/machine, purchasers of the product need not inquire whether it was made by a patented machine/process; they are generally not liable. Exception: if the patentee's claim covers a new composition or manufacture (a new product not previously known), sale or use of that product may constitute infringement of the product patent (Goodyear-related discussion). Assess whether the patent claim is to the product itself or only to the process/machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: If seller is connected with the use, vendor may be liable/enjoined
rubrics_metrics.description: If the person who sells is connected with the use of the machine, he is responsible as for an infringement; and if a court of equity has jurisdiction of the person, such a vendor may be enjoined, although the machine may be used beyond the jurisdiction of the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where mere purchasers of products are not liable, a vendor who has some connection to the illegal construction or use of the patented machine (e.g., joint construction, control, hiring out) can be restrained and held liable. Courts will look to the relationship between seller and user. (See Boyd v. McAlpin and related examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial-assignment rule for assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of an exclusive right to use a machine, and to vend the same to others for use, within a specified territory, authorizes the assignee to vend elsewhere, out of that territory, articles manufactured by such machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A territorial grant to use and vend does not necessarily prevent the assignee from selling the manufactured articles outside the assigned territory. Examine the terms of the assignment and relevant case law (Simpson v. Wilson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation of lawful use after expiration/extension nuances
rubrics_metrics.description: One who is in the lawful use and enjoyment of a patented machine at the time of the expiration of letters-patent may lawfully continue to use that identical machine, although the term of the letters-patent has been still further extended by a special act of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a party lawfully possessed and used a machine at patent expiration, special statutory extensions or later legislative acts have been held not to retroactively divest that right to continue using the identical machine; authority is cited (Bloomer v. McQuewan) though some judges dissented historically. Consider statutes and extensions carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: License-payment condition: nonpayment is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a license to use be conditioned on the payment of money, the use without such payment will be an infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a license expressly conditions the right to use on payment (royalties, fees), unauthorized continued use after failing to pay may subject the licensee to infringement liability and equitable relief. (See Brooks v. Stolley.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture/composition patents: acts constituting infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a 'manufacture' (or composition of matter) will be infringed by making, using, or selling the thing itself, or by importing it from a foreign country where it has been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the patented subject is the tangible product, the patentee's exclusive right extends to the thing itself; therefore, acts of making, using, selling or importing the patented product are infringing. Also note overlap: such patents often also cover the process of making the product. Evaluate whether the claim is to the product, the process, or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'using' for compositions — purchaser/consumer liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Strictly speaking, the use of a patented composition (e.g., a medicine) by consuming it could be an infringement, though holding purchasers or consumers liable would be an inconvenient restraint upon the public; purchasers are not ordinarily bound to inquire whether an article was made by the true proprietor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are reluctant to treat ordinary purchasers/consumers as infringers where they innocently buy and consume a patented composition; however, in strict theory a consumer could be liable. Sale to an agent of the patentee for the patentee's account is not itself an infringement but may be evidence of infringement when accompanied by other circumstances. Consider consumer knowledge, intent, and surrounding facts; see also English case on sewage-treatment process where accidental, rejected by-product use was held non-infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages presumption for statutory wrongful acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the law gives an action for a particular act, the doing of that act imports of itself a damage to the party; every violation of a right imports some damage, and if none other be proved the law allows nominal damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will recognize that the mere occurrence of a statutory infringing act can justify an action and at least nominal damages even absent proof of actual pecuniary loss. This supports standing to sue for acts such as unauthorized making, using, or selling under patent statutes.
